utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Groome, the Chamber was informed that you had a preliminary matter to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. Your Honour, on the 14th of January, 2013, P684 was admitted into evidence. The English translation of the document did not contain the translation of a handwritten note, and I'd refer the Chamber to T6698 to 6700, and a revised English translation was requested. We now have it and we would ask for the Chamber to grant us leave to replace the translation currently in e-court with this amended revised translation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The leave is granted and the Registrar is instructed to replace the new version of the translation to -- let me see. No. To replace the old version of the translation of P684 by the new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rose, I again would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of the testimony, but before Mr. Lukic resumes his cross-examination, I put on the record that Mr. Mladic is not in court today as we expected in view of your observations yesterday, Mr. Lukic, and that the Chamber received a signed waiver form signed by Mr. Mladic, and it is about the 18th of January. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that we will finish soon today, and I would kindly ask you to just bear for a little bit longer with me. You have your statement in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind and to look at paragraph 145 of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 145, you say that: "On the 27th of August, 1994, I accompanied General Wesley Clark, head of operations in the Pentagon to see General Mladic in Banja Luka." And you say, "General Mladic" insisted on a cease-fire, "pressed for a cease-fire to be followed by a political solution. General Clark advocated that a gesture should be made by the BSA such as withdrawal from an occupied area. I suggested further demilitarisation." On this occasion, also no concessions were sought from the Muslim side. Concessions were sought only from the Serbian side; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you discuss a document. I would like to look at the document in e-court. That's 8154, please. This is a report from the meeting of the 27th of August, and you recognise the format of the document, don't you? And at the bottom here in the report from this meeting, could you please look at item 5 at the bottom of the page, and there we can see that Mladic stated: "We have only 43.24 per cent of the territory," whereas the Muslims have 56.73 per cent with 37 towns. I would ask you this: Is it correct that each time the Serbs would receive less than 49 per cent of the territory according to the plans that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not party to the Contact Group. They kept themselves separate and distinct from any discussions we had with either of the warring parties. So I don't know what they had on offer at that time, and of course it was changing throughout the period that I was in Bosnia anyway. Different offers were being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the basis was to award territory to the Muslims? Was it by the number of the population, landownership or some other criteria, or do you know not know what the criteria were to determine these percentages?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I was not party to the Contact Group discussion, so I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just ask for your indulgence for a moment. We're now going to look at document 8155. We can see that this is a fax or a telegram being sent by Mr. de Lapresle to Mr. Annan, and in paragraph 149 of your statement you say: "On the 18th of September, 1994, I wrote both to General Mladic and General Delic, calling on them to immediately hold military actions ..." You warned them that if the fighting does not stop, I would be obliged to take all appropriate measures against their forces, including the use of air-strikes. What was the reaction to this by General Delic? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my discussion was with President Izetbegovic, and it was extremely negative. He was horrified to hear that I was threatening to use air-strikes against the Bosnian government forces, and I suspect he then made contact with the people on the NATO side to make sure that would not happen, but that's a supposition on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The position of the UNPROFOR was that the Serbs should not use the weaponry that they had handed in to the collection points controlled by UNPROFOR even in case of a Muslim offensive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D557 in e-court, please. This document consists of several sections. First is a report of the 16th of August from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan at the UN. I would like to look at page 4 of the document, the Protocol of Understanding. This protocol was drafted between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Karadzic. From paragraph 1, marked 1, first I think in my view we have two situations: One is that the UNPROFOR should withdraw. This is what the paragraph begins with. The second begins in line six of this paragraph, stating that in case the Muslims attack -- actually, in line 6 it states: [In English] "... in event of a Muslim attack on the Serbs which UNPROFOR is not able either prevent or stop immediately, the BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence." [Interpretation] General, in your view does that mean that the Serbs did have the right to take the weapons that they had handed in to the collection points or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it gave them the right to go and get those weapons back, and I was certainly not party to this particular agreement which when I saw it subsequently was somewhat of a surprise to me. We maintained the position that they had no right to come and collect the weapons from those weapon collecting points, which is why we on occasions called down air-strikes when they did so do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can we conclude that at the time when you called in air-strikes on Serb positions you had not seen this protocol?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of the protocol - can we look at it on the monitor, please - it states: [In English] "Neither the Serb nor the Muslim side is permitted to engage in military activities of any description, and this includes consolidation of trenches or their forward movement and similar activities." [Interpretation] General, is it correct that even after this date the Muslim forces did carry out offensives on Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They undoubtedly did so, particularly after the assault which they launched on the 18th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one moment, please. Need to look at the transcript of the 8th of October. I can't find it at the moment. Actually, I can't find the 65 ter number at the moment, or, actually, our 1D number. It's 1D551. We need to look at page 7581, please. Seventy-five. Line 13 on, up to line 19. You explained here, General, that the Muslims -- or that, rather, that NATO by that time had already changed its policies and that they were not prepared to use any force at all against the Bosnian government forces, or forces of the Bosnian government as it states here, even though the Muslim forces at that time were in direct violation of a NATO ultimatum. You did mention this before. What was this ultimatum from NATO? Could you please explain that a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ultimatum that had been given to both sides by NATO in 1993 was that there should be a zone on Mount Igman from which all military weapons and units would be excluded. It was known as the TEZ, total exclusion zone. And on this basis the Serbs who controlled most of the territory on Mount Igman withdrew their forces, relied on the UN and NATO to maintain the integrity of that total exclusion zone. As we've discussed, NATO's position subsequently changed, and when the Bosnian government forces attacked into that zone and slaughtered a number of nurses in a medical station, Serb nurses, NATO took no action in spite of my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go forward ten pages to transcript page 7591, please. We will be looking at lines 9 to 12. The Judge asked you -- actually, the question starts in line 10: [In English] "Now, would you say, General, that NATO's refusal to take action would have emboldened the Bosnian government to continue in that way?" The answer was: "It certainly would have done so and indeed it did so." [Interpretation] The Bosnian forces, knowing that they would not be bombed, did not pay much heed to your warning; is that correct? And they continued as if they had not been warned about their offences against the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at paragraph 167 of your statement now, please. In that paragraph you say that General Delic said that he should remove the units from the demilitarised zone. This is also a consequence of the awareness of the Muslim forces that no action would be taken against them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but we in fact ceased talking to General Delic on this subject, and we took the issue up with President Izetbegovic, and it was he who finally agreed to withdraw the Bosnian government forces back outside to a line outside the total exclusion zone. And he issued the orders to General Delic, and that finally happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 175 of your statement just briefly, please. Somewhere here at the end of the first half of the paragraph, you say that: "The first topic was the conflict in Bihac. Dr. Karadzic refused to recognise the safety zone the way it was recognised, as defined, and was insistent that his forces would continue to advance to destroy the Bosnian government Army's 5th Corps. Was the 5th Corps of the B and H Army a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess if there had been combat in the area and the 5th Corps were engaging the Serb side, they would have considered that to be a legitimate target in response. Unfortunately, the 5th Corps withdrew into the town, and that made it difficult for the Serb side to engage the 5th Corps elements without undue civilian casualties, and that is why the United Nations tried to prevent by calling in air-strikes civilian casualties in Bihac caused by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So UNPROFOR believed that at the moment when the Muslim forces entered the safe zone after participating in combat action, they stop being a legitimate military target. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether they were or not in the view of the Serbs made no difference to the United Nations approach. They were merely determined to halt fire being laid down in the civilian areas. That was our interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the previous answer started with, "I guess that if there had been." The ifs and ands are all there. That's one. Second, of course the Chamber would like to know 20 -- what was it? 24th of November, 1994, what rules, what Security Council Resolutions, what agreements were there, what actually happened for a fact, what then happened in response to that? I mean, that is all to give a proper judgement on what is legitimate. Is there a legitimate target? What does that mean? Can you engage every legitimate target with every means? That's all the questions that arise, which, of course, are not dealt with in such a way that it assists the Chamber to make its findings, at least with this witness. If it comes at a later stage, then of course we'll further hear from you, but it is if this, if that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I might be able to help with setting a certain baseline for subsequent discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Lukic would like you to do that, he's -- you're his witness at the moment. He's cross-examining you. I'm just commenting. If Mr. Lukic would invite you to do so, then we'll hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations at that time, as you know, had defined six safe areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and with the agreement of all the warring parties there would be no combat in or around those safe areas. Unfortunately, this was not adhered to, and when fighting broke out in these safe areas, particularly around Gorazde as we've heard, and Bihac, the United Nations' responsibility at that point was to deter further attacks against those safe areas. The exact boundaries of those safe areas were never particularly clearly laid down on a map, and a great deal of debate took place during my time, and particularly when the attacks occurred into Bihac, as to exactly where the boundary lay. In the end, it was decided that it was where the concentration of civilian populations were, and that would define the limits of the safe area, and that is when we -- when fire was laid down on these civilian occupied areas, that is when we called in NATO air-strikes. That was the basis on which our judgements were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you one short question but perhaps a difficult one. Was there any opinion formed within UNPROFOR and the UN about what would be the situation if the additional agreements between the parties would be violated? Would that mean that the underlying UN Security Council Resolutions would lose their validity or would be null and void, or would it just be that you step back and say the mutual agreement is violated. It's not binding upon the parties anymore. So the only remaining legal instrument which is now which is now ruling, which is now governing the situation is the UN Security Council, is it, or was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the case. That was the latter situation that you described was the line that we finally were obliged to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so if you violate your mutual agreements, fine, then what remains is the UN Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation, General. You used a term, "at the end." When was it that you actually determined that an inhabited or populated area would be what, in fact, you would be protecting? When was that in the end, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we never tried to protect because we didn't have the means for doing so. We were deterring attacks against, which is a different order of activity. But the moment at which we had decided this was to be the distinguishing feature of a safe area was after the attacks had been launched into Bihac, the 5th Corps Bosnian government forces had withdrawn into that area and there was fire beginning to be laid down in Bihac. At that point we decided that that was the definition we would use. So it was late November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it happen that NATO planes would bomb without the previous written consent by the Security Council? How did that mechanism function? You said that you would be seeking support of NATO planes in order to deter attacks. How would you go about getting permission for that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO reserved the right to fire without the authority of the United Nations, but only in self-defence, and by the November time, the Serb side had introduced high-technology, high-altitude complex ground-air defence systems, and NATO on occasions fired at these systems when they had been illuminated by hostile radar without authority of the United Nations. Otherwise, the only strikes that were made in Bosnia-Herzegovina were done [Realtime transcript read in error "don't"] with the authority of the United Nations. On the occasion of Bihac, NATO was unable to identify the targets that we wished them to engage, and therefore no air-strikes actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, can you help me with one clarification. You see on the transcript in the -- on page 11, lines 17 and 18 the sentence: "Otherwise, the only strikes that were made in Bosnia-Herzegovina were don't authority of the United Nations." I think there's -- it's not clear what is recorded here. Perhaps you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That should read "the only strikes that were made in Bosnia-Herzegovina were made with the authority of the United Nations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at paragraph 185 of your statement now, please. Here you talk about Dr. Karadzic, and then in the middle of the paragraph you say he demanded that the Croatian military leave their territory. What did the UNPROFOR do in respect of that request, because it's known, and you told us that some 5.000 soldiers from Croatia entered the territory controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly what this discussion was about and where these Croatian military were located, but I suspect it was probably in the area around Bihac, to the north of Bihac, or maybe to the west. But I don't recall this exact, precise discussion, the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it was in the Livno Duvno area, in fact. Do you recall -- you said here that you remember that conversation. Do you recall if anything was done in respect of this request? If not, we will just move on.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should move on, sir, because all dealings with the Croatian government were done by Zagreb and Mr. Akashi, not by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. From what I understood, UNPROFOR had two main tasks, the delivery of humanitarian aid and establishing peace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Initially, the Muslims welcomed the arrival of UNPROFOR and were grateful for the aid provided; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, the Muslims were opposed to the second task of the UNPROFOR, that is to establish peace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, of course, they were welcoming the UNPROFOR presence on -- for that reason as well, because they were in danger of being overrun by their opponents on the Serb side, but as they -- the situation stabilised and as they were being equipped and trained by NATO and the American side, they saw the peacekeeping effort as being an obstacle to them going back to military action in order to regain their lost territories by force of arms. So we -- the United Nations did indeed become an obstacle to their ambitions, their strategic ambitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I could add that by then the success of the United Nations aid delivery programme was such that the number of people dependent on humanitarian aid had greatly reduced and the Bosnian government felt that they were able to look after their own people without outside help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now briefly dwell on paragraph 199 of your statement. We're slowly coming to the end. You talked about your belief about the purpose of the siege of Sarajevo. Was there a large number of enemy soldiers being held, encircled in Sarajevo? Is it true that the Serbs were holding encircled the whole 1st Corps of the Bosnian Army? Would that be something that was justified?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly the Serb side had driven the Bosnian government forces into Sarajevo. How effective they were, I have no idea, but they certainly manned a defensive line which ran some 70 kilometres around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that the Serbs who were positioned around Sarajevo in many places were themselves surrounded by Muslim forces, that they in turn were also encircled?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't think of any particular location where that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If one were to look at the general area of Sarajevo. Perhaps you're not familiar with that, and I won't press that any further.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly didn't have a visibility of all the deployments of the warring parties throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I guess to the west and north of Sarajevo that could have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please bear with me. Thank you, General. Those were the questions I had for you, and thank you for answering them.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Bibles, could you give us an indication whether there is any need to further examine the witness and how much time that would take.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do have about -- I'd estimate maybe 30 minutes worth of questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please start. We'll take a break in approximately 10 minutes from now. No. Well -- Mr. Lukic, would it be of any use to have the normal length of sessions which is 75 minutes, which would give a better chance for Mr. Mladic to rejoin us after the break, because we would then resume later, and if he would have arrived by that time, he could immediately come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have no objection to that proposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we do not take the break after one hour as we do in the presence of Mr. Mladic, but that we continue until quarter to 11.00. You may proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General Rose, during cross-examination you were asked a series of questions about the Serb military operations in Gorazde in April of 1994. I'd like to return to this line of questioning, and in doing so, I'd like to start by showing you United Nations Security Council Resolution 824 referred to in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please bring P22 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General Rose, first I'll ask is this Security Resolution 824 as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we'd next like to go to page 2 of this exhibit, and specifically paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, specifically, I draw your attention to paragraph 4, particularly subsection (a), which declares the withdrawal of all Bosnian Serb military or -- military units.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to review that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you'd agree that this Resolution was dated on the 6th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd now like, Your Honours, to bring up P24, which would be UN Security Council Resolution 836 from the 4th of June, 1993, mentioned in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Does the document on the screen appear to you to be Resolution 836?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And if we could now go to page 3 and focus on paragraph 5. You have an opportunity to review this paragraph with respect to the UNPROFOR mandate with respect to the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm well aware of those [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. And particularly regarding the task to promote the withdrawal of military or paramilitary units other than those of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. General, in respect to Gorazde during your time in command, was UNPROFOR's mandate carried out in accordance with these Security Council Resolutions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of their ability it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to your -- turn your attention to paragraph 67 of your statement, and there you state: "At a meeting on 6 April 1994, in Pale, Radovan Karadzic said the Bosnian Serbs had no intention of capturing Gorazde town and merely wanted to retake villages on the right bank of the River Drina." Yesterday, Defence counsel showed you an order from General Milovanovic dated the next day, 7 April 1994, and sent to the commands of various corps within the Bosnian Serb Army. I'd like to bring up that order again, 65 ter 0923 -- excuse me, 09236. Specifically the second page and paragraph 2. It's starting where we see an order to the Bosnian Serb forces to enter Gorazde, and I believe the paragraph starts with "If a tactical opportunity" arises. General Rose, what do you assess the true objectives of the Bosnian Serb Gorazde offensive to be?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we tended to believe Dr. Karadzic's assertion that they were merely recovering their lost villages on the right bank of the Drina, but not having this intelligence in front of us at the time, had we done so, then of course we would have understood that their intention was to treat Gorazde in the way they subsequently treated Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution moves to admit 09236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P733, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P733 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, it triggers the following observation: The Chamber noted that you have not tendered any of the documents you used in evidence. Is that what you intended, or would you still want some of it to be in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that the documents will be introduced in the future as well, so we can introduce them in the future. I will -- I'm satisfied with the answers we got from the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, with respect to Mladic's involvement in the Gorazde offensive, yesterday you were shown a document, I believe it was yesterday, now in evidence as P731 - and I would ask that we bring that to our screens - which noted that General Mladic visited the zone of combat on 10 April 1994, and relayed a message to keep pushing energetically onward. General Rose, to place this statement in context, are you -- or could you describe as of the 10th of April of 1994, the state of the Bosnian government military forces in and around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time they had started to withdraw back into the town, leaving the town very much undefended, and it was about that time also that we called on air-strikes on artillery positions and armoured units that were firing on Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, General, turning to the bottom of page 18 of your statement and paragraph 77, would you agree now with the assessment that the Bosnian Army had collapsed and was in total retreat, that the soldiers appeared to have given up all armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly gave the impression of that. Whether this was done through a matter of tactics on their part or whether they had been forced into retreat by the Bosnian Serb side, we never really established.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During this time period, April of 1994, your statement, throughout this portion of your statement, you indicate you communicated both directly with Mladic and through others regarding the Bosnian Serb actions, and specifically in paragraph 78, you described that you sent a message warning of NATO strikes, that you received a response from him in paragraph 79. In paragraph 83, you detail specific warnings from Mladic about UN personnel. And in paragraph 85, you describe communications to Mladic warning him with respect to tanks.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All that figures with the events of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you have any concerns given this that the Bosnian Serb Army was confused over what you were asking them to do to avoid NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were quite specific in our demands, and they understood them fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In relationship to Gorazde, I would ask that we bring up 65 ter 09108. As this document is brought to our screens, I'd ask that you take a moment to review.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, General, does this appear to be an order from -- ultimately from Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be from Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And as we review this document, it appears that Karadzic met with a Russian official who suggested that international public -- the international public was coming around. And as we go through that, based on that perspective, that the Bosnian Serb forces had about three days to make maximum use of their military efforts.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did your observations of the subsequent activities in this time-frame reflect that this order was carried out?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had slowed down by then, but I think that was a result of NATO action. Looking at that letter, I suspect this is an interpretation of a statement made by President -- or Mr. Karadzic, and it was actually issued by the army headquarters based -- but based on a statement from Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 09108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P734, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P734 is admitted into evidence. Could -- could I ask one clarification on one of your previous answers, Mr. Rose. You said Gorazde, when they had withdrawn within the town, was more or less undefended. Now, a town or a city which is undefended has also a very specific legal meaning. I'm not bothering you with the interpretation of that, but part of it may be that, for example, it was declared that the opposite party could enter that town and would be free to do so. I mean, is this legal meaning that you had in mind or just factual that there was not much military activity in -- in engaging the party which was outside of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The latter. Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, on cross-examination you were shown a document referred to in paragraph 34 of your statement. Somewhat as a housekeeping matter and in response to the Trial Chamber's request, we have located a document -- the document here, which appears to miss the fax cover sheet, but contains perhaps the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we bring 10716 to the screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, if you have -- if you could take a few moments and review this first page.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to the second page, please. Is this --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And this was the same document --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- referred to in paragraph 34?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you have a perspective as to whether the first page in this document accurately depicts the events of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 10716 rather than 08137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections? Then -- yes, now, just for my recollection, was -- the previous one was not tendered yet, or was tendered but was a number assigned? Number P734 -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: My notes indicate that because of the concern about the first page that the other document was not MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Registrar, now having a full copy of the document and there's no need to have the cover page. I take it the content of that which is very short was read into the record anyhow, and that this is then the document attached to that cover page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 10716 shall be assigned Exhibit P735. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P735 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for clarification of report, it's 10716.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to turn your attention back to February of 1994. Tuesday, starting at transcript page 6880, you were asked a series of questions about the two commissions established to investigate the origin of the mortar bomb that landed in the Markale market on 5 February 1994, as well as questions on the methodology of the reports generated by these two commissions. General, are you in a position to comment extensively or in depth about these two commissions, their work or their reports with respect to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any further knowledge other than stated on the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you involved at all in the report writing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And would you consider yourself a technician or expert in these sorts of things?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, yesterday with respect -- or in the context of the JCOs operating in Gorazde, you were asked the following: "The person guiding the plane is a member of UNPROFOR. Would you agree with me that he, together with the pilot, makes up the team that is attacking a Serb target?" And your answer was: "That is correct." I'd like to ask a follow-up question to this: If the person guiding the plane makes up the team, is it a legitimate tactic to seize the person and then place him in a position that might be targeted by NATO?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly would have been a tactic employed and subsequently whether -- but I don't think it was employed at the Gorazde incident because they didn't take any JCOs as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Ms. Bibles, I opposed yesterday to "if" questions. You're doing exactly the same, and now we hear from the witness that the "if" does not materialise. So therefore that could be prevented by just putting factual questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I will cease that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Finally, General, Tuesday, at transcript page 6890, with respect to a Bosnian Serb position on a global peace agreement, you stated: "It was a very open proposal. It was a general proposal that was always on the table whenever we met with the Serb side." Would it, therefore, be accurate to characterise General Mladic as a peace monger?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. He was using advantageous military position to bring about an end to the conflict on his terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Mr. Lukic, it would be time for a break. Is there anything you would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You only have one question, and that would conclude the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I first, before we continue in this way, ask my colleagues whether they have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what we often do is that the Chamber's questions will be put before you have the last round. Judge Moloto has one or more questions. If we could squeeze this in, in, well, let's say, in the next five to six minutes I think it would be wise to continue. If not -- but I see Judge Moloto is confident that we'll be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: General, I just have one question I hope -- General, I just have one question, and I hope it will stay one. Yesterday at several locations you talked about the Muslims breaching a NATO ultimatum with respect to Mount Igman and that you called for NATO to -- to attack with an air-strike and NATO refused. I just want to ask on the roads here and just to be able to understand clearly, was it for you as -- as UNPROFOR to call for reaction as a result of a breach of a NATO ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed it was, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The reason that I'm asking the question is that in certain instances you, during your testimony, you appeared to make a clear distinction between NATO and UNPROFOR, and you said -- you would say, for instance, "No, that was for NATO to do. It was not for me." Now, I just -- are you able to explain to us why it was that you as UNPROFOR would act on behalf of NATO where NATO actually was not interested in acting in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original situation, sir, was that the NATO airpower was deployed in support of the United Nations mission on the ground, and as a result of independent action by NATO, this total exclusion zone could be established, but it was the United Nations on the ground who had to maintain the integrity of that exclusion zone and to report violations to NATO who we would then expect to take appropriate action. I never specifically called for air-strikes against the Bosnian. I had a general discussion with the American head of the NATO Air Forces in the eastern Mediterranean, and it was during this discussion that he informed me that NATO would never take military action against the Bosnian government side even if they breached a NATO ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, today we discussed the Resolutions 824 and 836. You told us that they served as the basis for your action, primarily in cases of breaches of local agreements. My question is this: If agreement between the warring parties was signed and one of the signatories was, for example, Mr. Akashi or another UN representative, was that supposed to be binding on UNPROFOR in the field as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was there to mediate in an agreement that had been signed between the two warring parties and the responsibility of UNPROFOR at that time was to try and guarantee the effectiveness of that agreement, but the United Nations forces on the ground were not in a war-fighting deployment. They were there purely to facilitate humanitarian aid. There was therefore a limit as to how much they could enforce any agreement. Sir, can I correct one statement I made previously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In response to the NATO ultimatum, I used the word "never." In fact, the NATO air commander said to me, The only time we would use force against the Bosnian government side was if your soldiers' lives were in immediate danger and the Bosnian government side continued their attack. At that point we may consider using an air-strike against them. But it was a very narrow situation that he described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Your soldiers'" meaning UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So "never" is quite -- was probably too absolute. It would have been "not normally."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And "your soldiers" being UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My soldiers being UNPROFOR peacekeepers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rose, unless the questions by the Bench have triggered any further need for questions -- they have not. This concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, staying with us for three days, having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who to address, but after the break, the next witness will be ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We take a break, and we will resume at -- let's take a break of 25 minutes, which is something in between of 20 and 30 minutes. We will resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I established that Mr. Mladic apparently has not yet returned. I do understand that the visit was slightly delayed, which may have caused his not yet returning. We first deal with the admission of evidence. Before we do so, the first one, of course, would be the statement of -- the 92 ter statement of Mr. Rose. Before we further discuss that, Ms. Bibles, the Chamber has considered, of course, the submissions by the Defence, and without going into every detail yet at this moment, on one issue the Chamber has reached a conclusion which is that the last two paragraphs, I think it's 218 and 219 that it's not much inclined to admit those two paragraphs. I'm not talking about 217 which is dealt with in the same comments by the Defence, but 218 and 219. The Chamber would strongly advise you to strike them from the document you seek to have admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we'll do that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll do that. You'll do that. Okay. Then are there any further submissions in relation to the associated exhibits? But perhaps we start with the -- with the statement itself. After we've now heard the evidence of the witness, Mr. Lukic, is there anything you'd like to add to the objections that were raised in your response to the motion in which the 92 ter statement was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, is there anything you'd like to further raise in relation to the 92 ter statement, any further reply to the Defence objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect to this statement, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay. The Chamber will decide on it. Now, associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides the matter immediately. We have of course had detailed submissions. The Chamber admits into evidence the 92 ter statement of Mr. Rose on the assumption that, as you just said, 218 and 219 are removed from it. I take it you'll upload it soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P736, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P736 is admitted into evidence. It is the statement of the 92 ter statement of General Rose without paragraphs 218 and 219. Associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Registrar, you could remind us what the 65 ter number was, because I take it that either -- would it keep the same number once a new version will be uploaded?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 28619 was previously MFI'd as P728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, about associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, over the break Mr. Lukic and I had an opportunity to go through the exhibits, both the associated exhibits. The exhibits which were used on cross-examination and exhibits -- any remaining exhibits used by the Prosecution, and I believe we have reached agreement, and I could go through that list or I could provide the list in whatever format that the Court would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you -- how many are there remaining? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Approximately -- it's over 20, Your Honour, less than 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Over 20. I suggest the following: You put them on a list. You give it to Mr. Registrar. He provisionally assigns numbers to them, and then we receive that list with the assigned numbers and the description of the document, of course, and then we'll decide on admission, and we do it in one swing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As my learned friend noticed, we did agree on -- on those documents, only I would like to have two more admitted from the associated exhibits list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please then -- I think two we could -- if you would just give the numbers then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's 8146 and 8147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 8146 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 8147.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D132 is admitted, and we will have the list of 20 soon. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be excused at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are excused Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I be excused as well, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope that not everyone leaves this courtroom this morning because we are the last ones to switch off the light. No. You're excused, Mr. Lukic, of course. Yes, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes. We're ready to call the next witness, but before he's brought in I would like to make a brief submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Harbour. Yes. Before he will be brought in, we will have to have the curtains down anyhow, because protective measures in place are face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym, which are leftovers from previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore when the witness enters the courtroom for those -- for that short moment, the curtain should be down. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Just one very brief matter. During proofing, the Prosecution provided this upcoming witness, RM046, with a list of names associated with the KP Dom Foca incidents that are charged, and we requested the witness to provide information -- any information he had on these individuals, and we will seek to tender the chart with his comments. Unfortunately, the translation of the chart is not yet complete, so the Prosecution requests that Your Honours allow us to conduct the direct examination today and briefly re-open for the sole purpose of laying a foundation for and tendering this chart on Monday, and we've already spoken with the Defence about this, and they've indicated that they have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case, it's agreeable to the Chamber as well to proceed as suggested. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom, curtains first being down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Officially we are in closed session now. We move into closed session for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness RM046, could I invite you to make the solemn declaration of which the text was already handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please be seated. Witness RM046 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- your testimony will be given under protective measures, that is face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym. Please keep in mind that if any of the questions would require in an answer to reveal information which again could reveal your identity, please do not hesitate to ask me to go into private session. Ms. Harbour, are you ready to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will first be examined by Ms. Harbour. Ms. Harbour is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Harbour, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please first have 65 ter 28549 on the screen. And this should not be aired to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Witness RM046, the Trial Chamber has explained the protective measures that apply to your testimony today, and I would like to ask you to take a look at this pseudonym sheet, and I direct your attention to where it says "Witness name." Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to where it says "Date of birth," could you confirm that that is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Harbour, would you please not forget to switch off your microphone when the witness answers any question. No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P737, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Witness RM046, do you recall giving statements to the Prosecution in April 1996 and in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you also testify in the Krnojelac case?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you meet with the Prosecution in November of 2012 to review the statements from April 1996 and October 1998, and also to review a short excerpt of your testimony from the Krnojelac case?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: At that time, did you provide another statement which contained corrections and clarifications of the prior statements and testimony and some additional information as well?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you meet again with the Prosecution to review and sign that new statement on the 19th of December, 2012?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Just prior to testifying today, did you again review each of your statements and identify some changes that you wished to make?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you review and sign a new proofing note containing only the corrections that you identified from the statements that you gave in 1996 and 2012? Did you review and sign that this morning?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and the truthfulness of your statements from 1996, from 1998, from 2012, and the corrections contained in the note that you signed this morning on the 18th of January, 2013?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Do you also affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of the excerpt of the testimony in Krnojelac that you reviewed which related to your experience in Kula?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If asked the same questions that you were asked while providing these prior statements and testimony, would you provide the same responses in substance?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: I would. They would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: In light of this, Your Honours, I would like to tender each of these prior statements, and I can list them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, it's commonly -- these documents are commonly shown to the witness. That's the standing practice before admission is sought. I don't know whether there's any specific reason why you do not, but it also may be that if there's -- if the Defence would agree on the 65 ter documents does not in any way contest that these are the statements given by the witness and it is the transcript of the testimony given by the witness and the proofing notes, then of course we could consider to proceed in that way, but without explanation, I think we should not proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If you'd like, I'll show each of these to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave two options. The second is more efficient, but you would need the response by the Defence. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not object to the way you proposed for things to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the Defence then accepts that the documents uploaded under the 65 ter numbers Ms. Harbour will use are -- in effect it will not challenge that these are the statements given by the witness and signed by the witness; is that correct, Mr. Stojanovic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we proceed along this procedure. Could you please mention the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The 1996 statement is 65 ter 28546.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P738, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P738 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The 1998 statement is 65 ter 28547.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P739, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The excerpt from the Krnojelac testimony is 65 ter 28548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P740, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The December 2012 statement is 65 ter 28628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P741, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Finally, the signed proofing note containing corrections is 65 ter 28652.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P742, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted under seal. Ms. Harbour, you did not make any distinction tendering under seal or not. One could wonder whether the transcript from the Krnojelac case would need to be admitted under seal because a pseudonym was used there as well, but I wanted to remain on the safe side, but could you please consider to what extent it's still needed to have that one under seal. Not necessarily now, but in the hours and days to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not necessary for that one to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P740, the status of P740 is changed into public -- a public exhibit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: The Prosecution also seeks to tender two associated exhibits which are associated to the December 2012 statements, and these are 65 ter numbers 14073 and 14137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 14073.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P743, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Any need to have it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 14137.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P744, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: And this can be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P744 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: With your leave, I would like to read a public summary onto the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. You have explained to the witness the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Witness RM046 lived in Foca leading up to the conflict. He was arrested on 11 April 1992, shortly after the conflict started. He was first detained in a military hangar in Livade before being transferred to the KP Dom Foca prison on 17 April. While at KP Dom, the witness observed mistreatment of detainees and was himself assaulted by guards and interrogated. The detainees were civilians, largely Bosniak, and included the elderly and physically and mentally ill. The witness observed a large number of people being taken from KP Dom, never to be heard from again. Others died from the bad conditions in the prison and inadequate medical care. After the conflict, the witness learned through his relationships with the victims' families and his involvement with a NGO and Missing Persons Commissions that many of the people he knew were at KP Dom were later exhumed from mass graves. Witness RM046 heard speeches by SDS politicians, Velibor Ostojic and Vojislav Maksimovic, on Radio Foca to the effect that Muslims and Serbs could not live together. He also heard a news report that Miroslav Stanic, the head of the SDS in Foca, had gone to Ratko Mladic to ask for military help. RM046 met several times with the KP Dom prison warden, Krnojelac, who told him that KP Dom officials received orders from the military command. In July 1993, RM046 was transferred to the Kula prison where conditions were similar. Here again, prisoners were mistreated. They performed forced labour, and they were killed. He was in Kula for one year before he was exchanged in June 1995. Could I please have exhibit 65 ter 18578 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Witness RM046, in your evidence you mention many rooms in which you were detained in KP Dom. Do you recognise what is depicted in this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes. It is the building number 1 where I was at the beginning of my detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. Sorry. No, this is the building number 2 where there were about ten solitary cells on the ground floor on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please move away from the microphone as we cannot understand everything. He is now too close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please sit a bit further away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would like to tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P745, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. P745 is admitted into evidence. Perhaps next time, Ms. Harbour, you could have the view rotated of a document which may make it easier for the witness to read any text on it, although it's of relative advantage, but he has recognised it now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Witness 046, in your 2012 statement, in paragraph 1, in the first bullet point you discuss several mass graves. How did you come to know about these graves? And if your response should be given in closed session, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Certainly. The mass graves were found after my release, and that is when I found out that they existed. To be more precise, it was on the 15th of June, 1995. I was exchanged under the auspices of the International Red Cross. Several years later, in 1998 more precisely, exhumations began in all of the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At first the exhumation and identification process in Bijeljina took place based on witness statements, clothes recognition, or identification papers that were found on the corpses or by visual examination. By 2001 or 2002, following the exhumations, there was an identification process undertaken by the international commission relying on DNA analysis in order to identify any killed persons precisely. If you wish, I may enumerate the more important mass grave sites. Most of the sites --

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: That's not necessary. What I would like for you to tell the Chamber is how you knew about these graves.

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: I learned about the graves from the relatives of those killed, their husbands, sons, et cetera. It was also through the state commission for the missing persons, the international commission, and of course through the NGO, the detainees association of Bosnia-Herzegovina which also engaged in looking for those who had been killed or went missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You list several of these graves in your statement. I'll just read them to you, and if there are any more that contained the bodies of KP Dom detainees, and let's limit it to the KP Dom detainees, if there were any more, please let us know after I have read to you the ones in your statement. Your statement speaks of Jama Piljak, Paunci, Buk Bijela, Previla and Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down because the interpreters are behind now. Could you now answer the question which was whether there are any other graves you are aware of where KP Dom detainees were buried.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, also the Buk Bijela tunnel, the Piljak pit, the mass grave in Dobro Polje, and the largest mass grave is the River Drina, which unfortunately was not mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 14072 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Witness RM046, the document that will shortly appear is entitled: "List of prisoners of war to be released from Foca prison because it was established in the proceedings that they have not committed crimes against the Serbian people." And it's dated 18 September 1992, signed by M. Kovac. Do you have any information about what happened to the people on this list?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them, or basically everyone -- perhaps we can go name by name. I could tell you what happened with them. One also needs to remember what took place in August and September in the detention centre. Whatever happened in the front lines had catastrophic consequences for us, the detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we limit ourselves to the people on this list. Not necessarily all one by one, but could you give a description of what happened to them or most of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. I think that this document was written later on the date after these people were taken out. This was on the 17th of September, 1992, when it went by rooms. From each room five to seven people were taken out. It wasn't 35 people but 45 people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to move back from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could I again ask you to be a bit further away from the microphone. Perhaps the microphones could be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I need to repeat what I said earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no need to do that. Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, everything that happened in the field at the front had a lot of negative repercussions for us who were in the camps. Specifically I'm talking about the Foca camp here, the KP Dom, but this happened in the other camps as well. I said that this list was drafted subsequently after a group of 45 people were taken out of the rooms that were there. I can mention a number of people who were taken out of my room. Number 18. I was there when this was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please focus your answer on the question; that is, what happened to them. What was their fate? You have now told us that they were taken out of the rooms the day prior to the date of this document. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were all taken out, and they were all killed. Many of them have been exhumed, and what is characteristic is that whenever a group of this size was taken out, it was never the case that they were killed and buried in the same mass grave. So we can find these people in a number of mass graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. If Ms. Harbour would be interested to know more, she will ask you about it. Your answer, therefore, is these people were not released but taken out of the rooms the previous day and were all killed. That is, I understand, your answer. Please proceed, Ms. Harbour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 14072 shall be assigned Exhibit P746.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: You've just told us that when something happened on the battle-field, that had a effect on the KP Dom detainees. And please answer my -- listen to my question and only answer the question. Were you ever informed by someone that KP Dom detainees were taken out in retaliation?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Formulated in that way that they were taken out in retaliation, no, but a Serb who found himself in prison later, he told me. I knew him well from before. He knew me as well. He told me, It's a good thing that you were not exchanged, because all the exchanges to date are suspicious. This was in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversations with someone named Dr. Dragovic about any of these issues?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes. The colleague that you mentioned, I know him. We worked together. At the beginning, he was engaged by Mr. Krnojelac to provide certain medical assistance to us, because at the time there were many people in the camp, some 6- to 700, according to some people in the camp, of all ages, and at one time when the offensive on Gorazde began, they probably suffered certain losses. And then this colleague that you mentioned told me that, It's very dangerous for you here. I asked him. This was in the medical station. I said, Why? He said, People -- three to five Muslims will be taken out and killed from here depending on their function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, first of all, if you want the witness to focus on your question, if he moves away from it, you should take him back to what your question was. Now, it may well be that all he tells us is what you had in mind to ask him, but that's unclear for the Chamber. Witness, the simple question was did you ever have any conversations on these issues. So the simple answer is yes, and then Ms. Harbour will ask further questions about specific matters she's interested in. Ms. Harbour, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to complete that last thought you had. You said that Mr. -- Dr. Dragovic told you three to five Muslims would be taken out and killed depending on their function. Did he say why they would be taken out and killed?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Yes. He clarified it. If any Serb is killed at the front, depending on his function -- actually, this actually did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If you could just clarify. When you say any Serb was killed at the front, depending on his function, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RM046
utterances.text: Simply it's an opportunity for the Serbs, the fact that they have Muslims available who are going to make up in this case for their casualties in battle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness until we re-open our direct examination on Monday, for the sole purpose of the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is understood. Mr. Stojanovic, we have another ten minutes to go unless you would prefer to have an early break. Apparently you prefer to start. Witness RM046, you'll now be cross -- you'll now be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, who is, and perhaps I should explain that to you, has waived his right today to be present in court. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just need your guidance now. Are we going to be working an hour or an hour and 15 minutes in this block?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I left it to some extent to you. If you have, for example, the expectation that by taking a break now Mr. Mladic would be able to attend the beginning of the cross-examination, feel free to ask for a break now. If you would prefer to start your examination, we'll then take a break in anything between 10 and 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Mr. Mladic will appear or not, but there is a possibility that he will appear, and in view of his wish to be in the -- in the courtroom, perhaps it would be a good idea to go on a break now. I also wanted to note that my short -- my cross-examination will be shorter than we announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shorter meaning what? Two minutes shorter or half an hour short or an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half an hour or more, Your Honour, that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's take a break first, but we have to move into closed session. But we'll take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00. We first turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Harbour, reading through the chart during the next break might assist you as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We could provide this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
